blocks.text: 1. LSH

blocks.alt: A vector goes through a locality-sensitive hash to land in a bucket

blocks.text: LSH covers a hashing based alternative approach to approximate nearest neighbor search, introducing a third fundamentally different search strategy.
It hashes similar vectors so they land in the same bucket most of the time.
2. A Third Distinct Strategy
HNSW used graphs; IVF used clustering; LSH instead uses hashing.
This gives a third fundamentally different way to narrow the search space before comparing vectors directly.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Algorithm","Core mechanism"],"rows":[["HNSW","A navigable graph of connected vectors"],["IVF","Clusters grouped around centroids"],["LSH","Buckets assigned by locality sensitive hashing"]]}

blocks.text: 3. What Makes A Hash Locality Sensitive

blocks.alt: Similar vectors land in the same bucket

blocks.text: An ordinary hash function scatters similar inputs randomly across buckets.
A locality sensitive hash instead deliberately places similar vectors in the same bucket.
4. Hashing As Bucket Assignment

blocks.alt: A vector goes through a hash function to produce a bucket ID

blocks.text: Every stored vector gets run through the same locality sensitive hash function to get a bucket label.
A query only needs to search vectors sharing that same bucket label.
5. Multiple Hash Tables For Recall
A single hash function can still miss some true neighbors that landed in a different bucket by chance.
Using multiple independent hash tables at once reduces the chance of missing a true match.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A vector missed by one hash table's bucket assignment still has a chance of being caught by a second or third independent hash table, since each uses a different random projection of the same vector space.

blocks.text: 6. The Speed Accuracy Knob

blocks.alt: Fewer tables are faster while more tables are more accurate

blocks.text: More hash tables improve recall but add storage and search overhead.
Fewer hash tables instead trade some accuracy for faster, lighter search.
7. LSH Versus Graph And Cluster Based Methods

blocks.alt: LSH uses hashing while HNSW or IVF use graph or cluster methods

blocks.text: Much like the IVF versus HNSW comparison, LSH tends to offer simpler implementation at the cost of lower recall than HNSW at comparable speed.
It represents a different point on the same underlying speed versus accuracy spectrum.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: LSH's simpler bucket based structure makes it easier to implement and reason about than HNSW's graph traversal, though typically at the cost of lower recall for a comparable amount of search time.

blocks.text: 8. When Hashing Struggles
Very high dimensional or unevenly distributed data can make good hash functions harder to design.
The right hash family has to match the actual structure of the embedding space.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Data characteristic","Effect on LSH"],"rows":[["Well distributed, moderate dimensions","Hash functions typically work well"],["Very high dimensional or uneven","Good hash function design becomes harder"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When LSH Is A Reasonable Choice

blocks.alt: Needing a simple, distributed-friendly method points toward LSH

blocks.text: Simpler infrastructure needs and moderate recall requirements suit LSH.
Maximum recall at similar speed, by contrast, often favors HNSW.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates hashing vectors into buckets and searching only within a matching bucket.

code.content:
import random

def random_hyperplane_hash(vector, hyperplanes):
    bits = []
    for plane in hyperplanes:
        dot = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(vector, plane))
        bits.append("1" if dot > 0 else "0")
    return "".join(bits)

random.seed(42)
dimensions = 8
hyperplanes = [[random.uniform(-1, 1) for _ in range(dimensions)] for _ in range(4)]

vectors = [[random.uniform(-1, 1) for _ in range(dimensions)] for _ in range(500)]
buckets = {}
for i, v in enumerate(vectors):
    bucket_key = random_hyperplane_hash(v, hyperplanes)
    buckets.setdefault(bucket_key, []).append(i)

query = [random.uniform(-1, 1) for _ in range(dimensions)]
query_bucket = random_hyperplane_hash(query, hyperplanes)
candidates = buckets.get(query_bucket, [])

print(f"Total vectors in collection: {len(vectors)}")
print(f"Query hashed to bucket: {query_bucket}")
print(f"Candidates in matching bucket: {len(candidates)}")
print(f"Number of distinct buckets formed: {len(buckets)}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the query landing in a bucket alongside only a small fraction of the full collection, narrowing the search before any distance comparison happens.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Using only a single hash table, missing true neighbors that landed in a different bucket.
Confusing an ordinary hash function with a locality sensitive one that preserves similarity.
Assuming LSH always matches HNSW's recall at the same speed without measuring the difference.
Applying a hash family poorly suited to the actual structure of the embedding space being searched.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: LSH hashes similar vectors so they land in the same bucket most of the time.
It offers a third fundamentally different strategy alongside HNSW's graphs and IVF's clustering.
A locality sensitive hash deliberately places similar vectors in the same bucket, unlike ordinary hashing.
A query only needs to search vectors sharing its own bucket label.
Multiple independent hash tables reduce the chance of missing a true neighbor.
More hash tables improve recall but add storage and search overhead, a tunable tradeoff.
LSH tends to be simpler to implement than HNSW, typically at somewhat lower recall.
High dimensional or unevenly distributed data can make designing good hash functions harder.
